newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch canals thaw, Belgian barging problems wane.
newsitem.headline: Dutch canals thaw, Belgian barging problems wane.

text.p: The steady thaw throughout northern Europe continued midweek, with iced-up Dutch waterways thawing and expected rain by the weekend likely to ease barging problems across the Benelux region.

Dutch water inspectors RIZA said the Rotterdam-Antwerp route was still only passable for barges in convoys behind ice breakers, but the Amsterdam-Rhine canals were now navigable for barges journeying alone, although floating ice remained a risk.
The Rhine was entirely free of ice in the Netherlands and Germany, RIZA said.

Temperatures in the region held above freezing point during the day, but mostly dipped below at night. However, the onset of rain, forecast by the Dutch Meteorological Institute for the end of the week in many parts was expected to speed up the thawing process.
Barge operators on Wednesday commented they were still experiencing problems on many key routes, but that journeys were becoming gradually easier.
"There's still the risk of (ice) damaging everything, but it is going a bit smoother," said one operator.
Operators added the biggest problems remained in Belgium, notably along the Albert Canal, linking Antwerp with the interior, which is currently blocked by ice.
"It means we can hardly get to the (Belgian/German) border which is a problem for a number of our customers," one barge operator said.
Operators were mostly confident that the major problems would be gone in about a week, assuming the weather did not change.

On Wednesday, independent U.S. forecaster Weather Services Corporation said temperatures in northwest Europe into the weekend would be above normal and stay "near to above normal" in six to 10 days time.
This should ease the delivery of 261,700 tonnes of gas oil, due after the expiry of the January futures contract of the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE).
Much of the product will come from Antwerp, with some additional supply from Amsterdam.
Barge operators predicted some problems in the first of the three five-day delivery "windows", but little thereafter.

The operators themselves welcomed the thaw, but not its immediate effect on freight rates. Barges still cannot enter many German canals and tributaries of the Rhine. Dortmund in the Ruhr area, for example, was still out of reach.
The result is that all barge traffic is concentrated on the Rhine itself, depressing rates.
"There are just no requests for destinations further inland, so there's more and more tonnage on the Rhine," one barge operator said.
